Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette: Chidi understood the blast not as a single moment but as a fractured sequence that still refused to settle. He remembered the heavy canvas tote of suit linings pressing against his hip as he walked through the central transit concourse. The first sound was a deep thud that vibrated through his boots, followed by a rolling wave of dust and screaming. When the debris settled, he was on his knees, searching for his phone, but his hands only found torn upholstery and the stunned faces of strangers. He remembered the sharp sting of glass in his palm, then nothing at all. There were entire stretches of that afternoon that simply would not return, no matter how hard he pressed his forehead against the bathroom mirror, straining for a glimpse of what he had missed. What remained played instead like a film that refused to pause—the way a man’s jacket flared upward, the sudden silence that swallowed the station announcements, the acrid smoke that coated his throat. He described those images with flat precision, feeling nothing. When the memories surfaced, they arrived stripped of everything but the cold, factual details, as if he were watching someone else’s misfortune. Chidi began mapping every doorway the moment he crossed it. At his tailor shop, he would step inside and immediately note the emergency exit behind the sewing machines, the side door leading to the alley, the front glass pane that opened to the street. He arranged his cutting table so his spine rested flush against the brick wall, because only then did the tension in his shoulders begin to ease. He stayed perched on the edge of his stool, listening to the hum of the neighborhood for any change in rhythm, certain that the next threat would arrive without warning. The silence where the trauma tried to speak grew heavy. Chidi found that staring at his phone screen for hours stilled the noise. He scrolled through videos and played strategy games until his eyes burned, using the digital glow as a buffer. The habits that formed around those nights bled into his work. When his supplier arrived late with a shipment of wool, Chidi found himself snapping over the delivery time, insisting on an impossible discount, manufacturing friction where calm would have been easier. He knew the argument simply pushed the day forward, giving him something else to fix. He stopped writing dates on his calendar. When a regular client asked if he could have a wedding suit ready by October, Chidi simply told him he was booked until spring, refusing to lock himself into a timeline that might collapse before it arrived. His shop grew quiet. The regulars stopped stopping by. He began to feel like a guest in his own neighborhood, drifting between streets where no one asked for his measurements, certain that his roots had been cut loose. He had come to believe he was a weak person for walking into that concourse without a second thought, for freezing when others ran, for trusting his judgment until the floor gave way. He could not trust that he would ever make the right call again. By the ninth month, the weight of the silence became unbearable. He found himself sitting in the back of his shop after hours, the cutting table cleared, the phone finally dark, just breathing through the panic that rose when the neighborhood fell quiet. He had come to know the shape of his own avoidance, the way it had hollowed out his friendships and stalled his business, but he no longer knew how to step through it. He sought counseling because the numbness had begun to feel permanent, and he was hoping, for the first time, to find a way to trust his own hands again without waiting for the next shock to catch him off guard.
